paragraphs: So they prayed, and Pallas Athena heard them. When they had finished their prayer to the daughter of great Zeus, they set off, like two lions prowling in the night through the armor and the blood-stained bodies of the fallen.

Hector did not let the Trojans sleep either. He too called together the princes and councillors of Troy, so that he could lay his plan before them. “Is there anyone,” he said, “who will do me a service for a great reward? I will tell you what it is. He will be well paid if he does it. I will give him a chariot and a pair of horses, the swiftest to be found at the ships of the Achaeans, if he has the courage for this task. He will also win endless honor. He must go to the ships and find out whether they are still guarded as before, or whether the Achaeans, now that we have beaten them, plan to flee and are neglecting their watches out of sheer exhaustion.”

They all kept silent. But among the Trojans there was a man named Dolon, son of Eumedes the famous herald, and rich in gold and bronze. He was ugly but a good runner, and he was the only son among five sisters. He now spoke up to the Trojans. “Hector,” he said, “I will go to the ships and spy them out. But first raise your scepter and swear to me that you will give me the chariot decked with bronze, and the horses that carry the noble son of Peleus. I will be a good scout for you and will not fail you. I will cross the whole host from one end to the other until I reach the ship of Agamemnon, where I expect the princes of the Achaeans are meeting to decide whether they will fight or flee.”

When he had finished, Hector raised his scepter and swore the oath. “May Zeus, the thundering husband of Hera, be my witness,” he said, “that no Trojan but you will ride behind those horses, and that they will be yours to do with as you like forever.”

The oath was empty, but it made Dolon all the keener to go. He slung his bow over his shoulder and put on the skin of a gray wolf as a cloak, with a cap of ferret skin on his head. Then he took a pointed javelin and left the camp for the ships. He would never come back with news for Hector. He left the horses and the troops behind and hurried on his way, but Odysseus saw him coming and said to Diomedes, “Diomedes, someone is coming from the camp. I cannot tell whether he is a spy or a thief out to strip the bodies of the dead. Let him pass us by a little, and then we can leap on him and catch him. If he outruns us, go after him with your spear and drive him toward the ships, away from the Trojan camp, so that he cannot get back to the town.”

With that they left the path and lay down among the corpses. Dolon suspected nothing and soon went past them. When he had gone about as far as a furrow plowed by mules is longer than one plowed by oxen (for mules work fallow land faster than oxen), they ran after him. He heard their footsteps and stopped, sure that they were friends from the Trojan camp, sent by Hector to call him back. But when they were only a spear’s cast away, or less, he saw they were enemies and ran as fast as his legs would carry him. The two gave chase at once. As two well-trained hounds press hard after a doe or a hare that runs screaming ahead of them, so the son of Tydeus and Odysseus hunted Dolon and cut him off from his own people. He had almost reached the ships and would soon have run into the outposts, when Athena gave fresh strength to the son of Tydeus. She did it so that no other Achaean could win the glory of hitting Dolon first and leave Diomedes only second. He sprang forward with his spear and called out, “Stop, or I will throw my spear, and then I will soon finish you.”

As he spoke he threw, but he missed on purpose. The spear flew over the man’s right shoulder and stuck in the ground. Dolon stood stock still, trembling and terrified. His teeth chattered and his face went pale. The two came up to him out of breath and seized his hands, and he began to weep. “Take me alive,” he said. “I will pay my own ransom. We have plenty of gold, bronze and wrought iron, and my father will give you a very large ransom out of it if he hears that I am alive at the ships of the Achaeans.”

“Do not be afraid,” answered Odysseus. “Put all thought of death out of your mind. But tell me, and tell me the truth. Why are you going about alone like this in the dead of night, away from your camp and toward the ships, while other men sleep? Do you mean to strip the bodies of the slain? Or did Hector send you to spy out what is going on at the ships? Or did you come here on your own whim?”

Dolon answered, his legs shaking under him. “Hector lured me away from my better judgment with his empty, flattering promises. He said he would give me the horses of the noble son of Peleus and his chariot decked with bronze. He told me to go through the darkness of the fleeing night, get close to the enemy, and find out whether the ships are still guarded as before, or whether the Achaeans, now that we have beaten them, plan to flee and are neglecting their watches out of sheer exhaustion.”

Odysseus smiled at him and answered, “You certainly set your heart on a great reward. But the horses of the descendant of Aeacus are hard for any mortal man to control or drive, except Achilles himself, whose mother was an immortal. Now tell me, and tell me the truth. Where did you leave Hector when you set out? Where are his armor and his horses? How are the watches and the sleeping places of the Trojans arranged? What are their plans? Will they stay here by the ships, away from the city? Or now that they have beaten the Achaeans, will they go back inside their walls?”

Dolon answered, “I will tell you everything truthfully. Hector and the other councillors are holding a conference at the monument of great Ilus, away from the general noise. As for the guards you ask about, no watch has been chosen to protect the host. The Trojans have their watchfires, because they must, so they are awake and urge one another to do their duty as sentinels. But the allies who have come from other lands are asleep. They leave the guarding to the Trojans, since their own wives and children are not here.”
Odysseus then said, “Now tell me this. Are they sleeping mixed in with the Trojan troops, or do they lie apart? Explain it so that I understand.”

“I will tell you everything truthfully,” replied Dolon. “Toward the sea lie the Carians, the Paeonian bowmen, the Leleges, the Cauconians and the noble Pelasgi. The Lycians, the proud Mysians, the Phrygians and the Meonians have their place on the side toward Thymbra. But why ask about all this? If you want to find a way into the Trojan host, there are the Thracians, who have only just arrived. They lie apart from the others at the far end of the camp, and their king is Rhesus son of Eioneus. His horses are the finest and biggest I have ever seen. They are whiter than snow and swifter than any wind. His chariot is decked with silver and gold, and he has brought his marvelous golden armor, of the rarest workmanship. It is too splendid for any mortal man to wear and fit only for the gods. Now take me to the ships, or tie me up securely here until you come back and have tested my words to see whether they are false or true.”

Diomedes looked at him sternly and answered, “Dolon, do not think that you will escape now that you are in our hands, however useful your information has been. If we ransom you or let you go, you will come back to the ships of the Achaeans some other time, as a spy or as an open enemy. But if I kill you and put an end to you, you will give no more trouble.”

Dolon was reaching for his beard to plead with him further, but Diomedes struck him with his sword in the middle of the neck and cut through both sinews, so that his head fell rolling in the dust while he was still speaking. They took the ferret-skin cap from his head, and the wolf skin, the bow and the long spear. Odysseus held them up high in honor of Athena, goddess of plunder, and prayed, “Accept these, goddess. We give them to you before all the gods on Olympus. Now guide us further, to the horses and the sleeping place of the Thracians.”

With these words he took the spoils and set them on a tamarisk tree. They marked the place by pulling up reeds and gathering tamarisk boughs, so that they would not miss it when they came back through the fleeting hours of darkness. The two then went on through the fallen armor and the blood, and soon came to the company of Thracian soldiers. They were sleeping, worn out by the day’s labor. Their fine armor lay on the ground beside them in three neat rows, and each man had his pair of horses next to him. Rhesus slept in the middle, and close by him his horses were tied to the top rim of his chariot. Odysseus saw him from a little way off and said, “Diomedes, this is the man, and these are the horses Dolon told us about, the one we killed. Do your utmost. Do not waste time on your armor. Loose the horses at once, or else kill the men yourself while I see to the horses.”

Then Athena put courage into the heart of Diomedes, and he struck the Thracians right and left. They groaned horribly as they were hacked down, and the earth was red with their blood. As a lion falls furiously on a flock of sheep or goats when it finds them without their shepherd, so the son of Tydeus fell on the Thracian soldiers until he had killed twelve. As he killed them, Odysseus came and dragged them aside by the feet, one by one, so that the horses could go forward freely and not be frightened as they passed over the dead bodies, since they were not yet used to them. When the son of Tydeus reached the king, he killed him too, which made thirteen. The king was breathing hard, for by the counsel of Athena an evil dream, the offspring of Oeneus, hovered over his head that night. Meanwhile Odysseus untied the horses, fastened them to one another and drove them off, striking them with his bow, because he had forgotten to take the whip from the chariot. Then he whistled as a signal to Diomedes.

But Diomedes stayed where he was, thinking what other bold deed he could do. He wondered whether to take the chariot where the king’s armor lay and pull it out by the pole, or to lift the armor out and carry it off, or whether he should kill still more Thracians. While he was hesitating, Athena came up to him and said, “Get back to the ships, Diomedes, or you may be driven there, if some other god rouses the Trojans.”
Diomedes knew it was the goddess and sprang at once onto the horses. Odysseus beat them with his bow, and they flew on toward the ships of the Achaeans.

But Apollo was not keeping a careless watch when he saw Athena with the son of Tydeus. He was angry with her. He went to the Trojan host and woke Hippocoon, a counsellor of the Thracians and a noble kinsman of Rhesus. Hippocoon started up from his sleep and saw that the horses were no longer in their place and that the men were gasping in their death agony. He groaned aloud and called his friend by name. Then the whole Trojan camp was in uproar, as the people kept rushing together, and they marveled at what the heroes had done before getting away toward the ships.

When they reached the place where they had killed Hector’s scout, Odysseus stopped his horses. The son of Tydeus leapt to the ground, put the blood-stained spoils in the hands of Odysseus, and remounted. Then he lashed the horses on, and they flew toward the ships, willingly, as if by their own choice. Nestor was the first to hear the beat of their hooves. “My friends,” he said, “princes and counsellors of the Argives, will I guess right or wrong? Still, I must say what I think. There is a sound in my ears like the beat of horses’ hooves. I hope it is Diomedes and Odysseus driving horses in from the Trojans, but I greatly fear that the bravest of the Argives may have come to some harm at their hands.”

He had hardly finished speaking when the two men came in and dismounted. The others shook their hands warmly and congratulated them. Nestor, knight of Gerene, was the first to question them. “Tell me, renowned Odysseus,” he said, “how did you two get these horses? Did you slip in among the Trojan forces, or did a god meet you and give them to you? They are like sunbeams. I know the Trojans well, for old warrior though I am, I never hold back by the ships. But I have never seen or heard of horses like these. A god must surely have met you and given them to you, for you are both dear to Zeus, and to Zeus’s daughter Athena.”

Odysseus answered, “Nestor son of Neleus, glory of the Achaeans, heaven, if it so wills, can give us even better horses than these, for the gods are far mightier than we are. But the horses you ask about have just come from Thrace. Diomedes killed their king along with the twelve bravest of his companions. Close by the ships we took a thirteenth man, a scout whom Hector and the other Trojans had sent to spy on our ships.”

He laughed as he spoke and drove the horses over the ditch, and the other Achaeans followed him gladly. When they reached the strongly built quarters of the son of Tydeus, they tied the horses with leather thongs to the manger, where the horses of Diomedes stood eating their sweet corn. Odysseus hung the blood-stained spoils of Dolon at the stern of his ship, so that they could prepare a sacred offering to Athena. They themselves went into the sea and washed the sweat from their bodies, their necks and their thighs. When the sea water had washed all the sweat off them and refreshed them, they went into the baths and washed again. After that they anointed themselves with oil and sat down to the meal. They drew wine from a full mixing bowl and poured a drink offering to Athena.
